page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question
Chemical Equilibrium, Acids and Bases · 2 marks

steps.label: The definition
lines: The decrease in the dissociation of a weak
electrolyte caused by adding a strong
electrolyte that has an ion common with it
is called the common ion effect.
steps.why: Adding the common ion raises that ion's concentration, and by Le Chatelier's principle the dissociation equilibrium shifts backward — so less of the weak electrolyte stays dissociated.
common_mistakes: Writing that the added salt must be weak. The added electrolyte is STRONG; the suppressed one is weak.
Leaving out the word common — the shared ion is the whole mechanism.
steps.memory_tip: Weak electrolyte + strong electrolyte with one ion in common: the common ion shifts the dissociation backward.
steps.margin_note: Name all three parts: weak electrolyte, strong electrolyte, common ion.

steps.label: The example
lines: shifts backward and the dissociation of

lines.text: The common ion CH₃COO⁻ suppresses the dissociation of CH₃COOH

steps.why: The acetic acid / sodium acetate pair is the textbook example: the acetate ion is common to both, and its raised concentration drives the weak acid's equilibrium backward.
common_mistakes: Writing the dissociation with a one-way arrow. It is an equilibrium: ⇌.
Naming a pair with no shared ion (e.g. CH₃COOH and NaCl) — the effect needs the common ion.
steps.memory_tip: Acetic acid and its own sodium salt — the same pair as the acidic buffer, seen from the equilibrium side.
steps.margin_note: Point at the common ion by name in the example.

insider_note: The example is a full mark and only earns it if the shared ion is named. Acetic acid with sodium acetate is the safe pair; a pair with no common ion cannot score, however well it is written.
